Each release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest is the only thing that tells a browser which files make up the current site.

The upload comes first because the switch is what makes the new names live. As soon as a browser loads the new manifest, it requests the files listed there. If those files were still uploading, the browser would get 404s or a half-updated page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the switch happens, so the change happens all at once.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. A page opened before the switch still holds the old manifest. It keeps requesting the old file names as it lazy-loads scripts, styles, and images. Deleting those files would break pages that are already open. Because each version has its own file names, old and new can sit side by side without overwriting each other. Every browser gets a complete, consistent set of files for whichever manifest it has.

Our releases happen in two steps. First, we upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images and so on) under a versioned filename, so new files never overwrite existing ones. Second, we update the manifest to point at those new names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what tells a browser which files to load. Once it points at the new names, any browser that fetches it will immediately request those files. If they aren't uploaded yet, those requests fail and users get a broken or unstyled page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the switch happens, so the switch takes effect for everyone at once.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Browsers that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still hold references to the old filenames. They keep requesting those files as they navigate or lazy-load parts of the page. If we deleted the old assets at release time, those users would hit missing files partway through a session. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new release.
